title: Fellowship in Minimally Invasive Gynecologic Surgery (FMIGS) — Curriculum and Instructional Design
author: Christopher Z. Mabini, DO, MSAEd — Inaugural MIGS Fellow
institution: PRIME Illinois St. Francis Hospital, Evanston, IL

blocks.text: This curriculum design presents a comprehensive curriculum for the Fellowship in Minimally Invasive Gynecologic Surgery (FMIGS) program at PRIME Illinois St Francis Hospital in Evanston Illinois and Metro Chicagoland area. The curriculum aligns with the program requirements set forth by the FMIGS Board and incorporates evidence-based approaches to ensure that fellows acquire advanced knowledge and surgical skills in minimally invasive gynecologic surgery (MIGS) per AAGL FMIGS program requirements and learning objectives. The curriculum integrates principles of adult learning theory using an instructional design and curriculum approach to enhance educational effectiveness, ensuring that learning experiences are self-directed, experiential, goal-oriented, and relevant to the fellows' professional practice (Knowles, Holton, & Swanson, 2015; Dick and Carey 2011). Detailed components such as context analysis, needs assessment, instructional plans, and evaluation strategies are provided to prepare fellows to serve as independent specialists and leaders in MIGS, addressing the healthcare needs, health equity and disparities impacting underserved populations and advancing the field through excellence in complex surgical management.

Minimally invasive gynecologic surgery (MIGS) has transformed women’s healthcare by offering surgical solutions that reduce patient morbidity, improve recovery times, and enhance overall quality of life (Nieboer et al., 2009). However, disparities in access to such advanced surgical care persist, particularly among low-income and underserved communities (Jacoby et al., 2011). Recent studies underscore the ongoing challenges in achieving diversity within MIGS fellowships and highlight systemic barriers that contribute to unequal access to minimally invasive surgical services (Hamilton et al., 2024; Isa et al., 2024; Sweterlitsch et al., 2024; Delara et al., 2020).

This FMIGS curriculum is specifically designed to train gynecologic surgeons who are committed to community-based care and the equitable healthcare delivery of MIGS and benign-complex disease management. By emphasizing the unique challenges and needs of low-income populations, the program aims to reduce healthcare disparities and improve outcomes for these communities (Williams et al., 2010).

Studies have shown that racial and ethnic minorities often experience higher rates of complications and readmissions after gynecologic surgery. For instance, Black women have been found to have a 30% higher risk of complications compared to White women in some studies. Minority women are less likely to receive minimally invasive procedures, which are associated with shorter hospital stays and faster recovery times. For example, Black and Hispanic women are up to 40% less likely to receive minimally invasive hysterectomies compared to their White counterparts. Some data suggest that Black women have a higher mortality rate following gynecologic surgery, which can be attributed to a combination of factors, including later-stage diagnosis and limited access to high-quality care.

The curriculum addresses these disparities by fostering a diverse cohort of fellows and promoting inclusive referral practices, as highlighted by recent literature identifying the importance of diversity and equitable training environments (Hamilton et al., 2024; Delara et al., 2020).

Research shows that women from low-income backgrounds have less access to MIGS. This disparity often leads to delayed care, progression of gynecologic conditions, and poorer outcomes compared to those with greater means. Black and Hispanic women face additional barriers, such as lower referral rates for MIGS and limited insurance coverage. Implicit biases within the healthcare system can also impact the quality of care and the surgical options offered to these women, resulting in fewer minimally invasive procedures and more complications.

To address these inequities, some low-income or community-based areas have developed targeted initiatives. These include expanding community health programs, enhancing the training of local healthcare providers in MIGS, and utilizing telemedicine to reach underserved populations. However, challenges such as limited funding and infrastructure persist, requiring continued advocacy and innovation.

Simultaneously, the fellowship is dedicated to advancing the field of MIGS by fostering and mentoring leaders with specialized knowledge in complex benign pathology and diseases, and expertise in the minimally invasive surgical management of these conditions (Advincula & Wang, 2009). Evidence from recent studies demonstrates that specialized MIGS training is associated with improved surgical outcomes and reduced complications, reinforcing the value of advanced training programs (Meyer et al., 2024; Gupta et al., 2022; Pfeuti et al., 2023).

The curriculum incorporates adult learning principles to ensure that educational experiences are relevant, practical, and engaging for adult learners (Knowles et al., 2015). By promoting self-directed learning, leveraging fellows’ prior experiences, and focusing on problem-solving and application, the program enhances the effectiveness of the learning process (Taylor & Hamdy, 2013). Furthermore, the program integrates simulation-based training and surgical intelligence tools, aligning with current trends in MIGS education that emphasize hands-on, technology-enhanced learning to improve surgical proficiency and patient outcomes (Hamilton et al., 2024; Pando et al., [year]; Levin et al., 2024).

Additionally, the curriculum addresses compensation trends and career development, ensuring that graduates are well-prepared for sustainable careers in MIGS. By understanding current compensation structures and addressing barriers to fellowship pursuit, the program supports fellows in achieving professional and financial success (Adedayo et al., 2024; Dassel et al., 2015; Traylor et al., 2019).

By addressing both the educational needs of fellows and the broader systemic issues within MIGS, the FMIGS curriculum strives to produce competent, compassionate, and socially responsible gynecologic surgeons. These surgeons are equipped to lead advancements in minimally invasive surgery, promote health equity, and improve patient outcomes across diverse communities.

A formal context analysis within the FMIGS curriculum ensures alignment with the needs of fellows, faculty, patients, and the healthcare institution. This analysis facilitates a tailored, competency-based approach that maximizes learning outcomes while being cost-effective and resource-conscious. By addressing the unique health needs of the community, available institutional resources, and adult learning principles, the curriculum becomes more relevant, impactful, and designed to produce highly skilled, well-rounded, and compassionate minimally invasive gynecologic surgeons.
Curriculum Context Analysis
Focus on Learners: Builds on fellows' existing skills and knowledge by incorporating adult learning principles such as self-direction and hands-on experiences.
Skill Development: Identifies gaps and strengths to target the development of complex surgical skills and decision-making abilities.
Facilities and Technology: Evaluates available surgical platforms (robotic, laparoscopic, radiofrequency ablation, etc.) to ensure curriculum feasibility and efficient resource use.
Faculty Expertise: Matches teaching responsibilities with faculty expertise to optimize learning experiences.

Each stakeholder plays a pivotal role in the success and growth of the FMIGS program. Fellows benefit from advanced training, while faculty ensure educational quality. Patients receive cutting-edge care, and community partnerships broaden fellows' exposure to diverse populations. Accreditation bodies and healthcare institutions provide the structural framework, while residents and medical students gain from peer learning. Policy makers and advocates, on the other hand, push for systemic changes, promoting equitable access to healthcare. Acknowledging the contributions and needs of each stakeholder ensures the program's alignment with broader healthcare goals, leading to continuous improvement in both education and patient outcomes.
Fellows: Primary Beneficiaries Seeking Advanced Training

Fellows are the core beneficiaries of the FMIGS program. They seek specialized training in minimally invasive gynecologic procedures, such as laparoscopic and robotic surgeries, complex hysteroscopy, and endometriosis excision.
Fellows drive the need for cutting-edge simulation-based training, research opportunities, and exposure to a wide range of clinical cases.
The fellowship equips them with leadership, teaching, and research skills, preparing them for roles in academic medicine or leadership positions in clinical practice.

The curriculum must prioritize fellows’ learning, offer exposure to complex surgical cases, provide simulation opportunities, and allow autonomy as fellows progress through the program. Fellow evaluations will shape program modifications, ensuring the program remains responsive to their evolving educational needs.
Faculty and Mentors: Deliver Education and Ensure Program Quality

Faculty are responsible for delivering didactic content, overseeing clinical training, and serving as mentors. They guide fellows in developing advanced surgical skills, clinical decision-making, and research capabilities.
Faculty ensure the program meets the educational objectives and accreditation standards. Their input is critical for curriculum development and modification based on ongoing evaluation.
Faculty members set the example for professionalism, patient-centered care, and lifelong learning, shaping fellows' approach to clinical practice and academic development.

Faculty development programs may be necessary to keep teaching methods current, particularly with advancements in surgical techniques and education technology. Faculty involvement in fellows' research projects, case-based learning, and surgical assessments is essential for maintaining program quality.
Patients: Receive Improved Access to Advanced Surgical Care
Patients benefit directly from the advanced training that fellows receive, particularly in areas like minimally invasive gynecology, which offers faster recovery times and lower complication rates.

Patients also play a role in the educational process, as fellows learn from real-world clinical experiences. Ethical considerations such as patient safety and informed consent are essential in training environments.
Fellowship programs expand access to specialized surgical care in the community by increasing the number of highly trained gynecologic surgeons.

The program must ensure patient safety through structured supervision of fellows and evidence-based clinical guidelines. Patient feedback can be integrated into fellow evaluations, ensuring care quality is maintained and improved.
Community Organizations: Collaborate in Outreach Programs
FMIGS programs often engage with community organizations for outreach, providing care in underserved areas and educating patients about gynecologic health.
Collaborations with community organizations allow fellows to participate in initiatives aimed at reducing health disparities, particularly in access to minimally invasive surgery.

These partnerships enrich the fellowship experience by exposing fellows to diverse patient populations and healthcare challenges. Community involvement also fosters leadership development, as fellows may take part in organizing health education programs or leading public health initiatives.
Accreditation Bodies: Ensure Compliance with Educational Standards

Program Compliance: Accreditation bodies such as ACGME, ABOG, and FMIGS Board oversee programs to ensure compliance with educational standards, including the breadth and depth of clinical and surgical training.
Continuous Improvement: Accreditation evaluations and site visits help identify areas for improvement, ensuring the program provides high-quality education that meets national standards.

The program must remain flexible and responsive to the requirements set forth by accreditation bodies. Compliance involves maintaining a robust curriculum, proper documentation, and quality assurance measures. Feedback from accreditation bodies may necessitate curriculum changes, faculty development, or adjustments in clinical training opportunities.
Healthcare Institution: Supports Program Implementation

The hospital or healthcare institution housing the FMIGS program provides resources such as surgical facilities, simulation labs, and clinical rotations. Institutional backing is crucial for the sustainability of the program.
The institution also plays a role in securing funding, managing faculty appointments, and maintaining compliance with legal and accreditation standards.

The program’s success is dependent on the institution’s commitment to investing in new technologies (e.g., robotic systems, simulation platforms) and ensuring the availability of diverse clinical experiences. Strong collaboration between the FMIGS leadership and the institution ensures that both educational and service objectives are met.
Residents and Medical Students: Benefit from Educational Interactions
Residents and medical students benefit from the expertise of FMIGS fellows through teaching, mentorship, and hands-on learning in clinical settings.
Exposure to advanced minimally invasive techniques during rotations or elective periods enhances the surgical skills of residents and informs their career decisions.

FMIGS fellows are integral to resident education, particularly in mentoring junior trainees during surgeries and providing lectures or case presentations. Interaction between fellows and residents promotes a collaborative learning environment, benefiting both groups and contributing to the overall educational culture of the institution.
Policy Makers and Advocates: Interested in Reducing Health Disparities
Policy makers and health advocates may use the program's success in providing advanced surgical care and outreach to underserved populations as a model for addressing health disparities.
Advocates for women’s health may push for policies that promote wider access to minimally invasive gynecologic surgeries, supported by data from fellowship-trained specialists.

Policy changes influenced by the outcomes of fellowship programs could impact the future structure of training programs, funding for advanced surgical techniques, or patient access to minimally invasive surgeries. Fellow involvement in community outreach and advocacy initiatives can highlight the program's role in addressing public health issues and reducing barriers to care.

A comprehensive needs assessment was conducted using data from local health departments, community health surveys, and national health statistics to identify gaps in gynecologic surgical care and the educational needs of the fellows.
Community Needs

The FMIGS fellowship program is dedicated to addressing the unique health needs and disparities present within the diverse communities of Evanston and the urban Chicago-land area. This commitment is underscored by the high prevalence of gynecologic conditions, limited access to advanced surgical care, cultural and language barriers, and health disparities that necessitate specialized training and targeted interventions. Incorporating specific demographic and diagnostic data from reliable sources emphasizes the program’s relevance and necessity.

Uterine Fibroids: In Evanston, African American women experience a higher prevalence of uterine fibroids compared to other ethnic groups, leading to increased morbidity and a greater need for surgical intervention (Baird et al., 2003). Studies have shown that Black women are three times more likely to develop fibroids than White women, often at a younger age and with more severe symptoms (Stewart et al., 2013). The FMIGS curriculum must equip fellows with specialized surgical approaches, including minimally invasive hysterectomies and myomectomies, to manage these complex cases effectively.

In Chicago, Hispanic women also exhibit a significant prevalence of fibroids, necessitating specialized surgical approaches to manage larger and more symptomatic fibroids effectively (Stewart et al., 2017). This underscores the importance of advanced MIGS training to address these challenges and improve patient outcomes in these communities.

Endometriosis and Chronic Pelvic Pain: In both Evanston and Chicago, up to 10% of women of reproductive age are affected by endometriosis and chronic pelvic pain—conditions that often require advanced surgical management to alleviate symptoms and improve quality of life (Bulun, 2009). Effective treatment of these conditions is essential for reducing long-term health complications and enhancing patient well-being. Advanced laparoscopic techniques taught in the FMIGS program are crucial for accurate diagnosis and effective management (Falcone & Flyckt, 2018).

sections.heading: Limited Access to Advanced Surgical Care

blocks.text: Underutilization of Minimally Invasive Surgery (MIS): Women from low-income and minority backgrounds in Evanston and Chicago are less likely to receive MIS procedures such as laparoscopic hysterectomies compared to their higher-income and White counterparts (Anderson et al., 2013). This underutilization results in longer recovery times, higher complication rates, and increased healthcare costs. A study by Johnson et al. (2017) found that minority women were 40% less likely to undergo minimally invasive hysterectomies. The FMIGS fellowship aims to bridge this gap by training surgeons in advanced MIS techniques and promoting their adoption within local healthcare facilities.

Insurance and Financial Barriers: St. Francis Hospital serves as one of the few safety-net hospitals in Chicago, catering to a substantial population of uninsured (30%) and underinsured (50%) patients (Illinois Department of Healthcare and Family Services, 2019). These patients face significant obstacles in accessing specialized surgical care, including MIS procedures, due to financial constraints and limited insurance coverage. Financial barriers often delay necessary treatments, leading to worsened health outcomes and exacerbating healthcare disparities (Artiga et al., 2019). The FMIGS fellowship program incorporates comprehensive training on navigating insurance complexities and advocating for policy reforms that expand coverage for minimally invasive procedures.

Health Literacy Issues: Approximately 25% of patients in Evanston and Chicago communities have limited health literacy, contributing to misunderstandings about gynecologic conditions and treatments (McCaffery et al., 2016). This barrier impedes effective communication between patients and healthcare providers, leading to decreased adherence to treatment plans and poorer health outcomes. Enhancing health literacy is essential for empowering patients to make informed healthcare decisions. The FMIGS curriculum includes training on communicating complex medical information in understandable ways to improve patient engagement and outcomes.

Language Barriers: Over 40% of the patient population in Chicago’s underserved communities are non-English speakers, primarily immigrants from Hispanic and Asian backgrounds (U.S. Census Bureau, 2020). These language barriers negatively impact the quality of care, as patients may struggle to communicate symptoms, understand treatment plans, and follow postoperative instructions (Flores, 2006). Providing language-appropriate resources, including trained medical interpreters and translated educational materials, is critical for ensuring equitable access to healthcare. The fellowship program incorporates training on cultural competence and the effective use of interpreter services to overcome these barriers (Betancourt et al., 2016).

Disparities in Cancer Screening: Minority women in Evanston and Chicago have lower rates of cervical cancer screening and higher mortality rates due to late-stage diagnosis (Benard et al., 2014). African American and Hispanic women are more likely to be diagnosed with advanced-stage cervical cancer, resulting in poorer prognoses (Rositch et al., 2014). This disparity highlights the need for outreach and education programs to improve screening rates. The FMIGS curriculum emphasizes the importance of proactive screening and early detection, training fellows to implement and advocate for community-based screening initiatives.

Delayed Care Seeking: Cultural beliefs and mistrust in the healthcare system contribute to delays in seeking care, especially among underserved populations in Evanston and Chicago (Jacobs et al., 2014). Historical injustices and ongoing discrimination have led to skepticism towards medical institutions (Scharff et al., 2010). Addressing these factors through community engagement, culturally sensitive care, and building trust can improve timely access to necessary treatments. The fellowship program includes training on culturally sensitive communication, community outreach strategies, and methods to build trust with patients.
Fellows’ Needs

To effectively address the community needs outlined above, the FMIGS curriculum must cater to the comprehensive training requirements of its fellows, including advanced surgical skills, cultural competence, research capabilities, and professional development.

Fellows require extensive training in advanced laparoscopic and robotic surgeries to manage complex gynecologic cases effectively (Advincula & Wang, 2009). Mastery of these techniques is essential for minimizing surgical complications and improving patient outcomes, particularly in cases involving uterine fibroids and endometriosis prevalent in the communities served.

sections.heading: Exposure to a Diverse Case Mix

blocks.text: Training across various clinical settings with a wide range of gynecologic conditions enhances surgical competence and prepares fellows to handle diverse patient populations (Azziz et al., 2009). Exposure to different case types fosters adaptability and comprehensive clinical expertise.

Effective Communication Skills: The ability to communicate effectively with patients from diverse cultural backgrounds improves patient satisfaction and adherence to treatment plans (Betancourt et al., 2016). Training in cultural competence ensures that fellows can provide respectful and individualized care, addressing the unique cultural and linguistic needs of patients in Evanston and Chicago.

Understanding Social Determinants of Health: Recognizing the impact of socioeconomic factors on health outcomes allows fellows to develop more comprehensive patient care plans (Artiga & Hinton, 2018). This understanding is crucial for addressing the broader context of patients’ health and improving overall care quality, particularly in underserved communities.

Evidence-Based Practice: Training in research methodologies enables fellows to contribute to advancements in MIGS and address health disparities through evidence-based interventions (Sullivan, 2011). Engaging in research fosters critical thinking and continuous improvement in clinical practices.

Focus on Health Disparities: Encouraging fellows to engage in research that explores and seeks to reduce disparities can lead to improved care for underserved populations (Braveman et al., 2011). This focus aligns with the program’s commitment to health equity and social responsibility.

Leadership Training: Developing leadership skills prepares fellows to advocate for patients and influence healthcare policies effectively (Blumenthal et al., 2012). Leadership training empowers fellows to drive positive changes within their institutions and the broader healthcare system.

Teaching Skills: The ability to educate residents, medical students, and patients fosters the next generation of healthcare providers and promotes informed communities (Skeff et al., 2010). Teaching skills are essential for fellows to disseminate knowledge and best practices in MIGS.

Identifying barriers to the transfer of learning from educational settings to clinical practice is essential for developing effective strategies to overcome them. Within the context of urban, diverse, and underserved healthcare environments, these barriers can be categorized into individual, organizational, and cultural/language-related challenges. Understanding and addressing these barriers will enhance the effectiveness of the FMIGS fellowship program and ensure that fellows can seamlessly integrate their acquired skills into clinical practice.
Individual Barriers

Heavy Clinical Workload: Fellows often juggle demanding clinical responsibilities alongside their educational activities. This dual burden can limit opportunities for focused learning and skill development, hindering the acquisition of advanced MIGS techniques (Lefebvre et al., 2016). Implementing structured scheduling and prioritizing educational activities within the fellowship program are necessary to mitigate this barrier. The FMIGS program adheres to the ACGME guideline that state “clinical and educational work hours must be limited to no more than 80 hours per week, averaged over a four-week period, inclusive of all in-house clinical and educational activities, clinical work done from home, and all moonlighting.

Risk of Burnout: High levels of stress and fatigue are prevalent among fellows due to the intense nature of clinical duties combined with rigorous training requirements. Burnout can impair learning, reduce performance, and negatively impact overall well-being (Dyrbye et al., 2017). Incorporating wellness programs and providing mental health support can help alleviate burnout risks.

Steep Learning Curve: Advanced MIGS techniques require significant practice and repetition. Inadequate exposure to these techniques within clinical rotations can hinder skill mastery (Donnellan et al., 2017). The FMIGS curriculum must ensure ample hands-on training opportunities through simulation labs and supervised surgical procedures to support skill acquisition.

Confidence Levels: Fellows may experience a lack of confidence in applying new skills in real-world clinical settings, especially when dealing with complex cases prevalent in diverse and underserved communities (Bandura, 1997). Building confidence through incremental learning, mentorship, and supportive feedback is crucial for effective skill transfer.
Organizational Barriers

Limited Access to Simulation, Cadaver Labs, Facilities: Although some institutions provide state-of-the-art surgical facilities, there may still be limitations in simulation resources specific to MIGS training (Stefanidis et al., 2013). Enhancing simulation-based training infrastructure is essential to provide fellows with the necessary environment to practice and refine their surgical skills.

Financial Constraints: Budget limitations in community hospital programs can restrict access to essential educational materials, conferences, and advanced training opportunities (Curet et al., 2017). Securing funding through grants, partnerships, and institutional support is vital to ensure that fellows have access to comprehensive educational resources.

Complex Healthcare Systems: Navigating intricate healthcare systems can pose challenges for fellows in implementing learned practices effectively (Woolf et al., 2015). Training on healthcare system navigation, including understanding referral processes and interdisciplinary collaboration, can enhance fellows' ability to apply their skills efficiently.

Resistance to Change: Institutional culture and established practices may resist the adoption of new approaches or technologies, impeding the integration of advanced MIGS techniques (Grol et al., 2013). Promoting a culture of continuous improvement and encouraging innovation within healthcare settings can help overcome resistance to change.
Cultural and Language Barriers

Language Differences: In underserved urban communities, a significant portion of patients are non-English speakers, primarily immigrants from diverse backgrounds. Communication difficulties can impede effective care delivery, making it challenging for fellows to apply their MIGS skills in a culturally competent manner (Diamond et al., 2019). Providing comprehensive language support services, including trained medical interpreters and multilingual educational materials, is essential for ensuring equitable care.

Cultural Misunderstandings: Lack of cultural awareness among fellows may lead to misinterpretation of patient needs and preferences, affecting the quality of care (Betancourt et al., 2016). Incorporating cultural competence training into the FMIGS curriculum will enable fellows to better understand and respect the diverse cultural backgrounds of their patients, fostering more effective patient-provider interactions.

Mistrust in Healthcare Providers: Historical injustices and perceived discrimination contribute to mistrust among minority populations in urban settings (Cuevas et al., 2016). This mistrust can lead to reluctance in seeking care and adhering to treatment plans. Training fellows in building trust through compassionate, respectful, and transparent communication is crucial for improving patient engagement and outcomes.

Health Literacy: Low health literacy affects patient understanding and adherence to treatment plans, especially in communities with diverse educational backgrounds (McCaffery et al., 2016). Fellows must be trained to assess and address health literacy levels, utilizing clear communication strategies and educational tools to enhance patient comprehension and involvement in their care. Fellows will begin to integrate social determinants of health (SDH) interviewing to assess for these barriers during history and intake.

chapters.title: Strategies to Improve Transfer of Learning

blocks.text: The FMIGS fellowship curriculum has been specifically designed to address barriers to the transfer of learning from educational settings to clinical practice. By integrating evidence-based strategies targeting individual, organizational, and cultural challenges within diverse and underserved urban healthcare environments, the program ensures that fellows are equipped to effectively apply their knowledge and skills in clinical practice. This approach aims to improve patient outcomes and reduce health disparities (Wong et al., 2018).
Enhancing Individual Learning

Dedicated time blocks for education are built into the weekly schedule, ensuring that learning activities such as lectures, workshops, and case discussions are prioritized without interference from clinical duties. Structuring these sessions into rotation schedules allows for consistent and predictable learning opportunities. An annual educational calendar is distributed to fellows, outlining all scheduled activities to facilitate advanced planning alongside clinical responsibilities (Owen et al., 2018).

The program adheres strictly to duty-hour regulations to ensure that fellows have adequate rest and do not experience excessive workloads. Mandatory rest periods and time-off policies are enforced to mitigate burnout and enhance learning capacity. Studies have shown that compliance with duty-hour policies improves resident well-being without compromising patient care (Bolster & Rourke, 2015). Flexible scheduling options, including adjusted shifts and part-time rotations, are available to accommodate individual needs and promote a healthy work-life balance (Goitein et al., 2015).
Simulation-Based Training

The curriculum incorporates advanced high-fidelity simulation training, providing fellows with access to state-of-the-art simulators that replicate real-life surgical scenarios. Regular simulation sessions allow fellows to continuously practice and refine their minimally invasive gynecologic surgery (MIGS) techniques in a controlled environment. Simulation-based education has been shown to enhance surgical skills and improve patient safety outcomes (Cook et al., 2011).

Structured practice sessions are embedded in the curriculum, enabling fellows to perform specific surgical tasks under direct faculty supervision with immediate feedback. These sessions include hands-on workshops and cadaver dissections seminars offered nationally, offering practical, supported settings for skill development. Deliberate practice with feedback is essential for acquiring expert performance in surgical skills (Ericsson, 2004). Attendance of at least one specialized workshops over course of fellowship, such as those offered at national conferences, is required to ensure comprehensive skill acquisition.
Mentorship and Coaching

Each fellow is paired with a dedicated faculty mentor who provides personalized guidance and support throughout the fellowship. Regular one-on-one mentorship meetings are scheduled, allowing mentors to offer feedback, discuss progress, and help fellows navigate clinical and personal challenges. Effective mentorship has been linked to increased job satisfaction, career advancement, and reduced burnout among medical trainees (Sambunjak et al., 2006).

The curriculum emphasizes peer learning, encouraging collaboration among fellows through structured group study sessions and collaborative research projects. Fellows engage in peer feedback systems to review each other’s performance and share insights, fostering a supportive, team-based learning environment. Peer-assisted learning enhances knowledge acquisition and promotes critical thinking skills (Henning et al., 2008).
Organizational Support

Investment in Educational Resources: The fellowship provides access to comprehensive educational materials, including textbooks, online courses, and surgical manuals. Simulation labs are fully equipped with essential MIGS equipment such as laparoscopic trainers and instruments, and the program will aim to continually invest in upgrading surgical equipment and educational technologies when able. Access to high-quality educational resources is crucial for effective learning and skill development (Leung et al., 2010).

Funding for Professional Development: Financial support is provided to fellows for attending regional and national conferences and specialized training opportunities suchas Global Congress of the AAGL, Bootcamp and attendance at the FMIGS webinars. Research associated costs (e.g., IRB, equipment,
publication) will also be funded by the fellowship. Aligning continuing education opportunities with fellows’ career goals ensures they have the resources needed to excel (Straus et al., 2013).
Curriculum Design

The curriculum incorporates self-directed learning modules, allowing fellows to pursue topics of interest at their own pace. Autonomy in learning fosters independent, lifelong learning and has been associated with improved educational outcomes (Murad et al., 2010).

Problem-based learning is a core component of the curriculum. Fellows engage in case-based discussions and simulations that mirror real-world clinical problems, facilitating active learning and critical thinking. This approach enhances retention and application of new knowledge (Dolmans et al., 2005).

The program incorporates interprofessional education sessions where fellows collaborate with healthcare professionals from other disciplines, such as anesthesiology, nursing, and radiology. Joint training exercises simulate multidisciplinary care scenarios, promoting teamwork and improving patient care outcomes. Interprofessional education has been shown to improve collaborative practice and patient outcomes (Reeves et al., 2016).
Addressing Cultural and Language Barriers

The curriculum encourages attendance to any hospital-sponsored workshops focused on cultural competence, addressing unconscious bias, and promoting sensitivity to patients’ diverse backgrounds. Fellows are encouraged to receive formal training in culturally tailored communication strategies, equipping them to effectively engage with patients from various cultural backgrounds. Cultural competence training improves patient satisfaction and healthcare outcomes (Lie et al., 2011).

Language services are available to support communication with non-English-speaking patients. Multilingual educational materials ensure patients have access to accurate, understandable information regarding their care. Fellows are encouraged to participate in language training relevant to the patient populations they serve, enhancing their communication abilities. Providing interpreter services improves clinical care for patients with limited English proficiency (Karliner et al., 2007).

Partnerships with Community Organizations: The program will invest effort and resources in establishing partnerships with local cultural centers, advocacy groups, and public health agencies to support community-based initiatives. These partnerships provide fellows with opportunities to engage in outreach activities, including health education and preventive screenings within underserved communities. Community engagement is essential for addressing health disparities and promoting public health (Wallerstein & Duran, 2010).

Patient Education Programs: Culturally tailored patient education materials are integrated into the clinical setting to address health literacy barriers. Fellows are trained in delivering patient counseling and education focusing on gynecologic conditions, treatment options, and prevention strategies. Improving health literacy is linked to better health outcomes and patient empowerment (Paasche-Orlow & Wolf, 2007).

Teach-Back Method Implementation: The program trains fellows in the teach-back method, ensuring patients understand their diagnoses and treatment plans. Fellows apply this method during patient encounters, with faculty observation and feedback to ensure proper execution. The teach-back method improves patient comprehension and adherence to treatment (Ha Dinh et al., 2016).

Motivational Interviewing Techniques: Motivational interviewing is integrated into the curriculum to enhance patient engagement and adherence to treatment plans. Fellows are encouraged to participate in role-playing exercises with faculty, residents, and/or allied health professionals to practice these techniques and receive performance feedback. These skills are applied during patient consultations to foster effective, patient-centered communication. Motivational interviewing has been effective in eliciting behavior change and improving health outcomes (Lundahl et al., 2013).
System-Level Interventions
Development of Quality Improvement and Clinical Pathways and Protocols

The curriculum includes standardized clinical pathways and protocols for common gynecologic procedures and conditions. Fellows are trained in applying these pathways through workshops and hands-on practice sessions, ensuring they implement evidence-based practices in clinical care. Standardized protocols reduce variability in care and improve patient outcomes (Panella et al., 2003). Outcomes are monitored using key performance indicators such as complication rates, procedure times, and patient satisfaction, with regular evaluations for continuous improvement.

Data collection systems are in place to capture relevant clinical and operational data. Fellows participate in regular data review meetings to analyze trends, identify gaps, and apply insights to improve clinical outcomes. This continuous feedback loop between data analysis and clinical practice enhances quality of care (Berwick, 2008).
Policy Advocacy

The program integrates advocacy training focusing on addressing social determinants of health. Fellows actively participate in projects aimed at reducing health disparities in their communities. They engage with policymakers at local and state levels, presenting data-driven proposals to improve healthcare access and outcomes for underserved populations. Physician advocacy is vital for advancing public health and promoting equitable healthcare (Gruen et al., 2006).

Health equity initiatives are embedded throughout the fellowship curriculum. Fellows work on projects focused on equitable resource allocation, addressing bias in healthcare, and improving access to specialized surgical care for underserved populations. Monitoring these initiatives through key performance indicators ensures the program meets its goals in reducing health disparities (Braveman et al., 2011).

chapters.title: Program Mission Statement, Goals and Objectives

blocks.text: Mission Statement

The mission of the Fellowship in Minimally Invasive Gynecologic Surgery (FMIGS) at PRIME Saint Francis Hospital is to provide an advanced, competency-based educational experience that prepares gynecologic surgeons to become leaders in complex benign gynecologic surgery, surgical innovation, research, and community health advocacy. The fellowship emphasizes equity-driven care, ensuring that trainees develop expertise in addressing disparities in gynecologic healthcare, implementing evidence-based minimally invasive surgical techniques, and engaging in high-quality research that advances the field.
Through a combination of didactic learning, hands-on surgical training, and scholarly research, FMIGS fellows will be prepared to:
Enhance patient care by implementing cutting-edge surgical techniques in minimally invasive gynecologic surgery.
Serve as clinical experts and consultants in the medical and surgical management of complex benign gynecologic conditions.
Contribute to the field through research and innovation, advancing the scientific knowledge of minimally invasive gynecologic procedures.
Train and mentor future generations of gynecologic surgeons through academic and professional development initiatives.
Overall Program Goals

The FMIGS program is structured to ensure that fellows achieve the highest standards in surgical proficiency, clinical excellence, research, and leadership. The program actively integrates evidence-based practices and relevant literature to address disparities in gynecologic health, particularly in underserved communities. Each of these goals is actively supported by evidence-based practices and relevant literature to ensure that FMIGS fellows are equipped to address the multifaceted challenges in gynecologic health, particularly within underserved communities.

Proficiency in Advanced MIGS Techniques: Fellows will attain proficiency in advanced minimally invasive gynecologic surgical techniques, including laparoscopic hysterectomy, laparoscopic myomectomy, advanced hysteroscopic procedures, and excision of deep infiltrating endometriosis (Donnellan et al., 2017). Fellows will develop expertise in robotic surgery and retroperitoneal dissection, applying best practices for nerve-sparing and fertility-preserving approaches.

High-Quality Patient Care: Fellows will implement evidence-based protocols to optimize perioperative care, postoperative recovery, and surgical outcomes. Standardized clinical pathways and continuous quality improvement initiatives will enhance patient safety and satisfaction (Rotter et al., 2010). Fellows will train as consultants and collaborate with interdisciplinary teams, including urogyn, colorectal, bariatric, and gyn oncology specialists, to manage complex benign gynecologic cases.

Resource for Underserved Patients: FMIGS fellows serve as specialized providers in community clinics, increasing access to advanced gynecologic care for underserved populations and reducing health disparities (Braveman et al., 2011).

Community Outreach: Participation in health fairs, screening events, and educational workshops enhances community health literacy and preventive care, fostering stronger community relationships (Anderson et al., 2015).
Health Education and Advocacy: Fellows will integrate health education and advocacy training to empower patients, addressing specific health literacy needs within communities (Ha Dinh et al., 2016).

Collaboration with Community Organizations: Fellows will partner with local cultural centers and public health agencies to facilitate targeted health initiatives, including preventive screenings and educational campaigns to improve women’s health outcomes (Koh et al., 2012).

Leadership and Ethical Practice: Leadership training modules and ethical decision-making workshops will cultivate leadership skills, preparing fellows to lead multidisciplinary teams effectively (Betancourt et al., 2016).

Educators and Mentors: Fellows will engage in structured teaching roles with medical students, residents, and allied health professionals to develop mentorship skills and foster a culture of continuous learning within the program (Blumenthal et al., 2012).

Advancing Health Disparities and MIGS Techniques: The program encourages fellows to conduct research focused on health disparities and innovative MIGS techniques, when able, contributing valuable insights and advancements to the field (Sullivan, 2011).

Scholarly Dissemination Fellows are required to submit their research findings for presentation at a national meeting and aim for publication in a peer-reviewed journal. Fellows are supported in publishing their research and presenting at conferences, enhancing their professional profiles and disseminating knowledge to broader audiences (Goldman et al., 2015).
The FMIGS program is committed to providing fellows with a comprehensive educational experience that emphasizes:
1. Medical Knowledge
Develop a thorough understanding of pelvic anatomy, physiology, and pathology relevant to benign gynecologic conditions.
Master the principles and applications of energy sources, instrumentation, and emerging surgical technologies in minimally invasive surgery.
Gain expertise in diagnosing and managing complex surgical complications, including ureteral injury, bladder injury, bowel injury, and massive hemorrhage.
2. Patient Care
Conduct comprehensive preoperative evaluations, optimizing patient selection and surgical planning.
Demonstrate proficiency in robotic-assisted laparoscopic procedures, hysteroscopic interventions, and advanced excisional techniques.
Implement enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) protocols, optimizing perioperative management to improve patient outcomes.
3. Research and Evidence-Based Practice
Develop critical appraisal skills to evaluate scientific literature and integrate evidence-based practice into clinical decision-making.
Complete at least one IRB-approved research project, with the expectation of submission to a peer-reviewed journal.
Engage in quality improvement initiatives, contributing to advancements in MIGS surgical techniques and patient care.
4. Teaching and Professional Development
Participate in resident, medical student education, and allied-health partners delivering structured didactic sessions, surgical mentorship, and skills-based workshops.
Gain experience in academic writing, oral presentations, and peer collaboration, preparing for leadership roles in medical education, hospital administration, and research.
5. Professionalism and Ethical Practice
Uphold the highest standards of ethical patient care, emphasizing informed consent, shared decision-making, and patient advocacy.
Demonstrate collegiality, integrity, and accountability in all professional interactions.
Maintain compliance with FMIGS accreditation requirements, institutional policies, and AAGL guidelines.

The FMIGS fellowship curriculum is structured to provide comprehensive education and training over two years following the completion of an obstetrics and gynecology residency (AAGL, 2020). The curriculum integrates clinical training, research, and innovative educational strategies to ensure fellows achieve clinical excellence, make meaningful community impacts, develop professionally, contribute to research, and engage in educational outreach. Each component is designed to ensure fellows gain proficiency in advanced minimally invasive gynecologic procedures, technological advancements, and evidence-based patient care.
Duration

Two years of continuous education and training post-residency with at least 20 months of unrestricted clinical training dedicated to minimally invasive gynecologic surgery (MIGS), encompassing diverse clinical rotations. All fellows will be required to start on August 1st. If an alternate start date is needed for administrative or personal reasons, FMIGS Board must be notified and requested for final approval which may incur an administrative fee.
Research:

Protected time for conducting research projects and engaging in scholarly activities that address community health needs and advance the field of MIGS. Each fellow is expected to complete a research project aimed at addressing health disparities, improving surgical outcomes, or other related topics relevant to the field of MIGS.
Curriculum components

The FMIGS fellowship curriculum integrates modern educational innovations rooted in adult learning theory, competency-based education, and surgical teaching practices. By emphasizing hands-on simulation, technology-enhanced learning, evidence-based strategies, personalized coaching, and competency-based assessments, the program ensures fellows develop the technical and professional skills necessary for excellence in minimally invasive gynecologic surgery. Each curriculum component is meticulously aligned with FMIGS educational objectives, supported by relevant literature, and designed for seamless implementation by educators and fellows.

Hands-on experience in diverse clinical settings under faculty supervision. Rotations will include specialized experiences in colorectal, urology, and reproductive surgery to enhance multidisciplinary collaboration

Fellows undergo rotations at core sites, exposing them to a wide range of cases and patient populations in multiple surgical specialties, thereby enhancing clinical versatility and adaptability (Braveman et al., 2011).

Utilization of AAGL/SGS/ACOG/ETC online resources for formal lecture-based learning, allowing integration of knowledge from national experts through weekly online lectures. Fellows will actively engage in journal clubs, case discussions, and live-streamed surgical education sessions.

Regular lectures, workshops, case-based learning, and seminars covering essential MIGS topics and related fields. Advanced topics such as complex retroperitoneal dissections, robotic-assisted techniques, and interdisciplinary surgical management will be emphasized.

Use of laparoscopic box trainers, AI-based models, and 3D printing for scenario-based surgical simulations. New additions include virtual reality-based surgical training modules and tele-mentoring/recorded surgeries for enhanced remote learning opportunities.

Integration and application of emerging technologies such as AI and 3D surgical simulations to enhance technical skill proficiency where appropriate (Higgins et al., 2021). Integration of augmented reality (AR) platforms will allow fellows to practice advanced surgical approaches before live patient procedures. Knowledge and skills in development of 3D printing in SIM training, patient education, and preoperative planning will be encouraged during the fellowship.

Emphasis on health disparities and innovative MIGS techniques, contributing to the advancement of the field (Sullivan, 2011). Fellows will participate in multi-institutional research collaborations and quality improvement initiatives targeting enhanced surgical safety.

Structured mentorship with faculty advisors for continuous guidance and professional growth. Dedicated research and clinical mentors will ensure fellows achieve competency in independent surgical practice and scholarly contributions.

Periodic assessments through case evaluations, surgical performance reviews, and competency-based evaluations (Ahmed et al., 2021). Competency tracking will be enhanced through standardized assessments and surgical video reviews.

Fellows will engage in leadership, teaching, and advocacy training through workshops, national conferences, and mentorship programs. Fellows will develop public speaking and communication skills essential for academic leadership and professional advocacy through lectures and grand rounds with sponsored OBGYN residency program and affiliates.

Active participation in health education initiatives, screenings, and partnerships with underserved communities (Anderson et al., 2015). Expanded partnerships with public health organizations will ensure fellows contribute to initiatives aimed at reducing gynecologic health disparities.
ACGME Curriculum Core Competencies

The curriculum objectives outlined align with the ACGME Core Competencies and FMIGS Educational Objectives, which are critical in ensuring that fellows in the FMIGS program develop the necessary skills to become competent, ethical, and effective minimally invasive gynecologic surgeons.
MK1: Demonstrate in-depth understanding of pelvic anatomy and pathophysiology

Deep knowledge of pelvic anatomy and related pathophysiology is essential for the safe and effective performance of minimally invasive gynecologic surgeries. This understanding allows fellows to navigate complex anatomical areas, such as those involved in endometriosis or pelvic organ prolapse surgeries.
MK2: Stay current with advancements in MIGS and apply evidence-based practices.

The field of Minimally Invasive Gynecologic Surgery (MIGS) is constantly evolving with new techniques and technologies, such as robotics and laparoscopy. Staying updated on advancements allows fellows to incorporate the latest, evidence-based practices into patient care, leading to better outcomes.
MK3: Understand the epidemiology and management of gynecologic conditions prevalent in the communities served.

Understanding the epidemiology of gynecologic conditions in specific populations ensures that care is tailored to the patient population, addressing prevalent conditions like fibroids, ovarian cysts, and endometriosis. This is key to providing effective, population-specific healthcare.
PC1: Provide compassionate, appropriate, and effective patient care.

Compassion and appropriateness in care are essential to developing trusting relationships with patients. Patient-centered care improves patient satisfaction and adherence to treatment plans, leading to better outcomes
PC2: Perform advanced MIGS procedures with proficiency and safety

Surgical proficiency ensures that fellows are able to perform advanced procedures such as laparoscopic hysterectomies, myomectomies, and endometriosis excision with minimal complications. Safety is paramount to reduce morbidity and mortality associated with surgeries.
PC3: Develop individualized patient care plans addressing social determinants of health.

Recognizing and addressing social determinants of health, such as socioeconomic status, access to care, and education, allows for a more holistic approach to patient care. This leads to personalized treatment plans that can improve health outcomes, especially for underserved populations.
PBLI1: Engage in continuous self-assessment and reflective practice

Reflective practice encourages fellows to assess their own performance and seek continuous improvement, which is crucial for lifelong learning. This skill helps surgeons stay adaptable and improve their techniques over time.
PBLI2: Utilize quality improvement methodologies to enhance patient care

Incorporating quality improvement methodologies (like Plan-Do-Study-Act cycles) enables fellows to systematically assess and enhance the care they provide, leading to higher standards of clinical care and improved patient outcomes.
PBLI3: Incorporate feedback to improve clinical performance
Actively seeking and using feedback from mentors, peers, and patients fosters an environment of growth and improvement. This is crucial in refining surgical techniques and communication skills.
ICS1: Communicate effectively with patients, families, and healthcare teams

Strong communication skills are essential for ensuring that patients fully understand their diagnoses, treatment options, and postoperative care instructions. Effective team communication is also critical for safe and coordinated care, especially during surgeries
ICS2: Demonstrate cultural competence in interactions with diverse populations

Cultural competence helps fellows navigate cultural differences and language barriers, improving trust and rapport with patients from diverse backgrounds. It is critical in reducing health disparities and ensuring equitable care.
ICS3: Educate patients and communities about gynecologic health

Patient education empowers individuals to take an active role in their health, leading to better preventive care and adherence to treatment plans. Public education also helps raise awareness of important issues like cancer screening and reproductive health.
PROF1: Uphold ethical principles and professional responsibilities

Ethical practice is the foundation of trust between healthcare providers and patients. Upholding ethical principles, such as confidentiality, informed consent, and patient autonomy, ensures that care is patient-centered and ethically sound.
PROF2: Demonstrate respect, compassion, and integrity

Respect, compassion, and integrity are essential for building strong therapeutic relationships with patients. These qualities also foster a positive work environment and are necessary for team-based care.
PROF3: Advocate for patient access, equity, and quality care

Fellows must be advocates for their patients, ensuring they receive high-quality care regardless of their background. This includes advocating for better access to care for underserved populations, addressing inequities, and ensuring patients have the necessary resources to receive appropriate treatment.
SBP1: Understand and navigate healthcare systems to optimize patient care

Knowledge of healthcare systems (insurance, hospital systems, care coordination) allows fellows to navigate these structures efficiently, ensuring that patients receive timely, cost-effective care without unnecessary delays or barriers.
SBP2: Collaborate with community resources to address patient needs

Working with community organizations helps address non-medical factors that impact health, such as housing, nutrition, and social support. This collaboration is particularly important for vulnerable populations that may face significant barriers to care.
SBP3: Recognize and address health disparities and social determinants of health

Fellows need to be aware of health disparities that affect different populations and work to minimize these disparities through individualized care, outreach, and advocacy. Addressing social determinants of health leads to more comprehensive, equitable care.
10. Instructional Plan Model
Learning Strategies:

Fellows create personalized learning plans, engage with the FMIGS Core Reading List, and attend relevant conferences to address individual knowledge gaps (Knowles et al., 2015). E-learning platforms, including SurgeryU and interactive self-assessment quizzes, will supplement traditional learning strategies.

Hands-on clinical rotations and simulation-based environments facilitate real-time learning and skill application, following Kolb’s experiential learning model (Kolb, 2014). Fellows are encouraged to engage in structured self-reflective debriefing sessions after surgical cases to reinforce skill acquisition and clinical decision-making.

Monthly case conferences, journal clubs, and research meetings promote peer collaboration and collective problem-solving (Johnson & Johnson, 2009). Multi-institutional collaboration will be encouraged to broaden exposure to advanced surgical techniques.

Curriculum alignment with clinical practice through problem-based learning and case studies ensures practical application of knowledge (Merriam & Bierema, 2013). Fellows are encouraged to integrate case-based studies to be associated with fellows' actual operative experiences, integrating real-world applications.
Building on residency training with peer teaching and customized teaching approaches tailored to fellows' backgrounds (Knowles et al., 2015).

Clear, measurable learning objectives and outcome-based assessments ensure focused and effective learning (Knowles et al., 2015). Competency-based progression ensures that fellows advance at an appropriate pace based on demonstrated mastery of skills. The FMIGS Milestones assessment (Appendix) will ensure learning objectives align with the fellows’ evolving competency levels. These milestones aim to provide a framework for assessment of the essential skills and knowledge expected of a participant graduating from the fellowship and aid in the identification of any surgical or educational deficiencies with ample time for remediation. These milestones are not designed to cover all aspects of benign gynecologic surgery, but rather to help ensure that fellows graduating from each program will achieve competency with key surgical and clinical skills.

Promotes teamwork through interdisciplinary collaboration and group learning activities, fostering a supportive educational atmosphere (Johnson & Johnson, 2009). Integration of interprofessional learning sessions with nursing, anesthesiology, and surgical subspecialties will enhance collaborative care models.
Key Adult Learning Theories Integrated into the Curriculum:

This theory emphasizes that adults learn best when they are involved in planning their learning and when the learning is relevant to their experiences and needs. According to Knowles (1984), adult learning is characterized by self-directed learning, where learners take the initiative in diagnosing their learning needs, formulating goals, identifying resources, and evaluating outcomes. Knowles (1984) also emphasizes that adults bring a wealth of life experience that they integrate into their learning process, using these experiences as a foundation for absorbing new knowledge. Moreover, adults tend to be motivated by the practical application of knowledge, especially when it relates directly to solving real-life problems or improving their personal and professional lives (Knowles, 1984). The FMIGS curriculum incorporates self-directed learning, problem-solving exercises, and interactive case-based teaching strategies to optimize adult learning outcomes.

This theory posits that learning occurs through experience and reflection. In medical education, this would manifest in case-based learning, simulation activities, and hands-on clinical practice. Kolb’s (1984) experiential learning theory argues that learning is a continuous process grounded in experience. Kolb (1984) outlines a four-stage learning cycle: concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualization, and active experimentation. Learners move through these stages by first having a direct experience, reflecting on it, conceptualizing what they have learned, and then applying this new knowledge in practical scenarios. According to Kolb (1984), this process is iterative and builds upon the learner’s previous experiences. Simulation training, surgical video review, and post-operative debriefing sessions follow this model, reinforcing skill acquisition through direct experience and reflection.

This theory focuses on learners constructing their own understanding and knowledge of the world through experiences and reflecting on those experiences. Constructivist learning theory posits that individuals actively construct knowledge by interacting with their environment and building on prior knowledge. Piaget (1972) and Vygotsky (1978) both contributed to the understanding of constructivism, emphasizing that learners actively create their understanding based on personal experiences and that learning is a social process influenced by interactions with others. This theory encourages learners to become active participants in their learning rather than passive recipients of information (Piaget, 1972; Vygotsky, 1978). The FMIGS program applies this by integrating problem-based learning, surgical case discussions, and research-focused inquiry to encourage critical thinking.

This theory explains how critical reflection on one’s beliefs and experiences can lead to a profound change in perspective, which is important in fields like palliative care where end-of-life considerations challenge many existing beliefs. Mezirow’s (1991) theory of transformational learning describes how adults can experience deep shifts in their worldview through critical reflection. According to Mezirow (1991), transformational learning occurs when individuals critically examine their assumptions and beliefs, leading to a fundamental change in their perspectives and behaviors. This theory highlights the importance of discourse and reflection in fostering transformative learning experiences that can significantly alter an individual’s approach to life and work (Mezirow, 1991). This is applied in structured feedback sessions, ethical decision-making workshops, and patient-centered care discussions.

Emphasizing learning through observation and interaction with others, this theory may be used in settings like interdisciplinary team-based care in hospice education. Bandura’s (1977) social learning theory emphasizes the role of observational learning, imitation, and modeling in behavior acquisition. According to Bandura (1977), individuals learn by observing the actions of others and the consequences that follow, integrating these observations into their behavior. This theory underscores the significance of social interaction and environmental factors in shaping an individual’s learning processes and behaviors. Fellows will participate in interdisciplinary surgical teams, observational learning through mentor shadowing, and peer-assisted learning models.
Innovations in Surgical Fellowship Teaching

Incorporation of AI ‘assistants’ to create a conversational and interactive learning tool that is aimed at enhancing problem solving, reference, research, technical skills and procedural retention (Higgins et al., 2021; Ahmed et al., 2021).

E-Learning Platforms: Secure platforms like SurgeryU host surgical videos, interactive case reviews, and self-assessment quizzes, facilitating flexible, self-paced learning (Frontiers in Surgery, 2024; Knowles, 1984).

Video-Assisted Surgeries: Access to recorded procedures allows fellows to review and learn at their convenience, aligning with adult learning theories emphasizing autonomy (Frontiers in Surgery, 2024). Real-time telementoring will be integrated into surgical education, allowing faculty oversight during procedures remotely.
Evidence-Based Learning Strategies

Implementation of retrieval practice and interleaved practice sessions enhances long-term knowledge retention and adaptability in surgical decision-making (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006; Rohrer et al., 2020).
Coaching and Mentorship Models
Personalized coaching improves performance by providing individualized feedback and fostering self-directed learning, aligning with adult learning principles (Richards et al., 2022).
Competency-Based Education (CBE)

Focus on skill mastery through competency checklists and proficiency assessments ensures fellows achieve essential surgical competencies before advancing (Ahmed et al., 2021). FMIGS milestones tracking (Appendix) ensures objective evaluation of fellow progression.
Adult Learning Theory and Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD)

Training within the ZPD framework ensures fellows perform procedures under structured supervision, gradually achieving independent proficiency (Richards et al., 2022). Progression from observation to active participation is tailored to each fellow’s competency level.

FMIGS Year 1: Independent Didactic Plan

Focus Areas: Over the course of Year 1, the curriculum covers essential topics such as pelvic anatomy, fibroid management, endometriosis excision, hysteroscopy, pelvic organ prolapse, and advanced suturing techniques.

Simulation Training: Each section includes detailed simulation activities to reinforce procedural skills, ranging from basic hysteroscopic techniques to advanced laparoscopic suturing in complex anatomical areas.

Case-Based Learning: Fellows engage in in-depth review and discussion of complex cases, allowing them to apply theoretical knowledge to real-world scenarios and improve their surgical decision-making.
Outcome Assessments: Fellows are evaluated on their technical proficiency and decision-making throughout the curriculum, ensuring they meet the rigorous standards required by the FMIGS program.

I. Module Overview and Objectives

This module ensures that fellows not only gain theoretical knowledge but also practical skills essential for modern clinical research. By mandating the completion of these peer-reviewed and internationally recognized online courses, the fellowship program fosters a culture of excellence, critical thinking, and evidence-based practice—key elements for future leaders in the field.

sections.heading: Module Title: Research Methodology and Scholarly Communication

blocks.text: Overall Objectives:
Equip fellows with essential skills in scientific writing, statistical analysis, systematic reviews/meta-analyses, clinical trial design, and clinical data management.
Enhance the fellows’ ability to produce high-quality, peer-review–ready research outputs.
Foster the integration of research methodology into ongoing scholarly projects throughout the fellowship.
Learning Outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this module, fellows will be able to:
Scientific Communication: Compose clear and compelling scientific manuscripts, grant proposals, and other research documents.
Biostatistical Analysis: Critically apply descriptive and inferential statistical methods to analyze and interpret clinical data.
Systematic Reviews: Design and conduct systematic reviews and meta-analyses adhering to established guidelines.
Clinical Trials: Understand the design, implementation, and interpretation of clinical trials to inform evidence-based practice.
Data Management: Implement robust data management practices to ensure data integrity and compliance with regulatory standards.

IV. Implementation Strategy

First quarter of first year: Fellows are expected to complete the aforementioned modules early in the fellowship period. This allows the skills acquired to be integrated and applied to ongoing research projects.
Faculty mentors will guide fellows in applying these methodologies to their individual research projects, facilitating hands-on experience and continuous feedback.
Each fellow must submit evidence (i.e., certificates of completion) for all six courses as part of their final fellowship portfolio.
Annual progress reviews will be held to ensure timely completion of courses.
Research Projects 2 Year Timeline
Identify Research Interests:
Conduct a needs assessment aligned with community health priorities.
Engage with faculty mentors and peers to refine research questions.
Develop IRB Research Proposals:
Draft detailed research protocols, including objectives, methodology, and ethical considerations.
Submit proposals to the Institutional Review Board (IRB) and address any feedback.
Initiate Research Activities:
Begin pilot studies or preliminary data collection as applicable.
Establish research teams and assign roles.
Secure necessary resources (e.g., equipment, funding, access to data).
Literature Review and Methodology Refinement:
Perform a comprehensive review of current literature to support the research framework.
Refine research methods based on preliminary feedback and pilot results.
Data Collection Commencement:
Initiate systematic data collection following the approved protocol.
Monitor data quality and adherence to the study design.
