Program Evaluation Process Overview

The Program Evaluation section is essential to ensure the continual improvement and accountability of a Fellowship in Minimally Invasive Gynecologic Surgery (FMIGS) program. This section outlines the methods and purpose behind evaluating the fellowship's performance, identifying areas for improvement, and ensuring alignment with accreditation standards.
Methods of Program Evaluation

Surveys are a key tool in gathering comprehensive feedback from three core groups: fellows, faculty, and patients. These surveys provide insights into both the educational experience and the impact of the fellowship program on patient care.

Fellow Surveys: Fellows are asked to evaluate their educational experience, the quality of didactic teaching, the adequacy of simulation training, and overall mentorship and faculty support. Surveys should focus on key areas such as:
Learning environment: Are learning objectives clear and being met?
Simulation experiences: Are simulation-based sessions and skills labs sufficiently preparing them for clinical practice?
Support and feedback: Do fellows feel supported by mentors, and is feedback constructive and frequent?
Quality Improvement Process Template for FMIGS Program

Objective: To establish a structured, ongoing quality improvement process aimed at enhancing the Fellowship in Minimally Invasive Gynecologic Surgery (FMIGS) program by identifying gaps, updating curriculum, and continuously adapting to emerging trends in minimally invasive surgery.
1. Introduction to Quality Improvement

Purpose: The primary objective of program evaluation is to continuously improve the FMIGS program by identifying areas where fellows require additional training, enhancing faculty mentorship, refining the curriculum, and updating simulation and didactic workshops based on real-time data and emerging trends.
Frequency of Review:
Quarterly review of progress and implementation of adjustments.
Annual comprehensive evaluation of the entire program to inform long-term planning.
2. Step-by-Step Process for Quality Improvement
Step 1: Data Collection and Analysis
A. Identifying Gaps
Data Sources:
Survey Results: Collect data from fellows, faculty, and patients via semi-annual surveys focusing on curriculum, training needs, clinical outcomes, and mentorship quality.
Surgical Outcomes: Review data from EMR systems tracking fellow performance, complication rates, and clinical outcomes.
Feedback Sessions: Evaluate input from structured feedback sessions with fellows and faculty to identify areas requiring additional training or mentorship.
Analysis Process:
Quantitative Analysis:
Identify specific areas where fellows are underperforming based on competency scores from evaluations and surgical outcomes.
Compare key performance indicators such as complication rates, time to procedure completion, and patient satisfaction scores against benchmarks.
Qualitative Analysis:
Analyze feedback for common themes related to gaps in the curriculum, issues in mentorship, and deficiencies in technical skills.
Report Creation:
Develop quarterly reports that detail identified gaps in the curriculum, skills training, mentorship, and patient care practices.
Include recommendations for action based on data analysis and feedback received.
Step 2: Enhancing Surgical Training
A. Curriculum and Training Adaptation
Continuous Curriculum Review:
Based on the identified gaps, modify the curriculum to enhance training where needed. Examples include:
Advanced Techniques: Introduce new simulation modules to address deficiencies in specific surgical techniques (e.g., ureterolysis, DIE excision, suturing).
Emerging Trends: Incorporate recent developments and new techniques in minimally invasive gynecology, such as AI-assisted surgery or advanced robotic platforms.
Fellow-Specific Training Plans:
For fellows identified as needing additional training in specific areas, develop individualized learning plans that include:
Enhanced Simulation Sessions: Increase exposure to high-complexity cases in a simulated environment.
Targeted Didactics: Offer additional didactic sessions focused on areas of difficulty, such as endometriosis excision or advanced suturing.
Regular Evaluation and Feedback:
Continuous monitoring of fellow progress through real-time assessments, direct observation, and follow-up surveys.
B. Strengthening Faculty Mentorship
Faculty Development:
Provide faculty with feedback from surveys and assessments, highlighting areas where mentorship may need improvement (e.g., more consistent feedback, better structured guidance).
Conduct faculty development workshops that focus on effective mentorship strategies and offer mentorship tools that align with program goals.
Improving Mentor-Fellow Interaction:
Increase the frequency and structure of mentorship meetings to ensure that fellows receive timely, actionable feedback.
Step 3: Updating Simulation and Didactic Training
A. Simulation-Based Learning Updates
Identify Key Gaps in Skills Training:
Use feedback from simulation assessments to determine areas that need improvement. Examples might include difficulties with tissue handling, advanced suturing, or laparoscopic navigation.
Introduce New Simulation Scenarios:
Develop new or modify existing simulated surgical cases to address gaps. Examples of updates:
Case Complexity: Introduce more complex surgical scenarios that challenge fellows with deeper infiltrative endometriosis (DIE) or significant pelvic adhesions.
Multidisciplinary Simulations: Incorporate scenarios that involve managing multi-organ involvement (e.g., bowel, bladder, ureter) and require advanced interprofessional communication.
Expand Simulation Technology:
Use emerging technologies such as virtual reality (VR) or 3D-printed models to simulate more complex anatomical challenges.
B. Enhancing Didactic Content
Interleaved Learning:
Continuously update didactic content to include the latest research findings and emerging techniques.
Provide case-based didactic sessions that challenge fellows to apply knowledge to complex scenarios.
Simulation-Didactic Integration:

Ensure that didactic teachings are directly linked to simulation experiences. For example, a didactic session on deep infiltrating endometriosis should be followed by a corresponding simulation that allows fellows to apply their learning in a realistic, controlled setting.
3. Implementation of Action Plans
A. Action Plan Development
Targeted Interventions:
Following the identification of gaps, develop targeted interventions that focus on curriculum adjustments, simulation upgrades, and enhanced mentorship efforts.
Examples of interventions:
Adding additional simulation time for challenging cases such as DIE excision.
Offering one-on-one mentorship sessions for fellows struggling with specific procedural competencies.
Establish Timelines:
Set realistic timelines for the implementation of changes. For example:
Curriculum Modifications: Within the next 3 months, update simulation modules.
Faculty Development: Conduct faculty development workshops within 6 weeks.
B. Monitoring and Adjusting the Action Plan
Continuous Monitoring:
Regularly track the progress of the action plan through quarterly reviews.
Measure the effectiveness of interventions using follow-up surveys and performance metrics.
Adjustments Based on Feedback:
Adapt the action plan based on feedback from ongoing evaluations. For example, if faculty development initiatives do not result in improved mentorship, revisit and refine the training offered.
4. Documentation and Reporting
A. Quarterly Quality Improvement Report
Content:
Overview of identified gaps and areas of improvement.
Summary of actions taken to address these gaps.
Evaluation of the effectiveness of interventions.
Recommendations for continued improvements.
Distribution:
Distribute the report to fellows, faculty, and program directors during quarterly meetings.
Make the report available to institutional leadership and accreditation bodies as needed.
5. Conclusion

Continuous Quality Improvement: The FMIGS program will adhere to a structured, data-driven process of continuous quality improvement. This includes a consistent evaluation of fellow performance, faculty mentorship, and training outcomes, ensuring that the program evolves to meet emerging challenges and remains aligned with the highest standards of minimally invasive gynecologic surgery.

Commitment to Excellence: Through continuous monitoring and targeted interventions, the FMIGS program is committed to providing a world-class training experience that equips fellows with the skills and knowledge necessary to excel in their careers.

Quality Improvement Process Template for FMIGS Program

Objective: To establish a structured, ongoing quality improvement process aimed at enhancing the Fellowship in Minimally Invasive Gynecologic Surgery (FMIGS) program by identifying gaps, updating curriculum, and continuously adapting to emerging trends in minimally invasive surgery.
1. Introduction to Quality Improvement

Purpose: The primary objective of program evaluation is to continuously improve the FMIGS program by identifying areas where fellows require additional training, enhancing faculty mentorship, refining the curriculum, and updating simulation and didactic workshops based on real-time data and emerging trends.
Frequency of Review:
Quarterly review of progress and implementation of adjustments.
Annual comprehensive evaluation of the entire program to inform long-term planning.
2. Step-by-Step Process for Quality Improvement
Step 1: Data Collection and Analysis
A. Identifying Gaps
Data Sources:
Survey Results: Collect data from fellows, faculty, and patients via semi-annual surveys focusing on curriculum, training needs, clinical outcomes, and mentorship quality.
Surgical Outcomes: Review data from EMR systems tracking fellow performance, complication rates, and clinical outcomes.
Feedback Sessions: Evaluate input from structured feedback sessions with fellows and faculty to identify areas requiring additional training or mentorship.
Analysis Process:
Quantitative Analysis:
Identify specific areas where fellows are underperforming based on competency scores from evaluations and surgical outcomes.
Compare key performance indicators such as complication rates, time to procedure completion, and patient satisfaction scores against benchmarks.
Qualitative Analysis:
Analyze feedback for common themes related to gaps in the curriculum, issues in mentorship, and deficiencies in technical skills.
Report Creation:
Develop quarterly reports that detail identified gaps in the curriculum, skills training, mentorship, and patient care practices.
Include recommendations for action based on data analysis and feedback received.
Step 2: Enhancing Surgical Training
A. Curriculum and Training Adaptation
Continuous Curriculum Review:
Based on the identified gaps, modify the curriculum to enhance training where needed. Examples include:
Advanced Techniques: Introduce new simulation modules to address deficiencies in specific surgical techniques (e.g., ureterolysis, DIE excision, suturing).
Emerging Trends: Incorporate recent developments and new techniques in minimally invasive gynecology, such as AI-assisted surgery or advanced robotic platforms.
Fellow-Specific Training Plans:
For fellows identified as needing additional training in specific areas, develop individualized learning plans that include:
Enhanced Simulation Sessions: Increase exposure to high-complexity cases in a simulated environment.
Targeted Didactics: Offer additional didactic sessions focused on areas of difficulty, such as endometriosis excision or advanced suturing.
Regular Evaluation and Feedback:
Continuous monitoring of fellow progress through real-time assessments, direct observation, and follow-up surveys.
B. Strengthening Faculty Mentorship
Faculty Development:
Provide faculty with feedback from surveys and assessments, highlighting areas where mentorship may need improvement (e.g., more consistent feedback, better structured guidance).
Conduct faculty development workshops that focus on effective mentorship strategies and offer mentorship tools that align with program goals.
Improving Mentor-Fellow Interaction:
Increase the frequency and structure of mentorship meetings to ensure that fellows receive timely, actionable feedback.
Step 3: Updating Simulation and Didactic Training
A. Simulation-Based Learning Updates
Identify Key Gaps in Skills Training:
Use feedback from simulation assessments to determine areas that need improvement. Examples might include difficulties with tissue handling, advanced suturing, or laparoscopic navigation.
Introduce New Simulation Scenarios:
Develop new or modify existing simulated surgical cases to address gaps. Examples of updates:
Case Complexity: Introduce more complex surgical scenarios that challenge fellows with deeper infiltrative endometriosis (DIE) or significant pelvic adhesions.
Multidisciplinary Simulations: Incorporate scenarios that involve managing multi-organ involvement (e.g., bowel, bladder, ureter) and require advanced interprofessional communication.
Expand Simulation Technology:
Use emerging technologies such as virtual reality (VR) or 3D-printed models to simulate more complex anatomical challenges.
B. Enhancing Didactic Content
Interleaved Learning:
Continuously update didactic content to include the latest research findings and emerging techniques.
Provide case-based didactic sessions that challenge fellows to apply knowledge to complex scenarios.
Simulation-Didactic Integration:

Ensure that didactic teachings are directly linked to simulation experiences. For example, a didactic session on deep infiltrating endometriosis should be followed by a corresponding simulation that allows fellows to apply their learning in a realistic, controlled setting.
3. Implementation of Action Plans
A. Action Plan Development
Targeted Interventions:
Following the identification of gaps, develop targeted interventions that focus on curriculum adjustments, simulation upgrades, and enhanced mentorship efforts.
Examples of interventions:
Adding additional simulation time for challenging cases such as DIE excision.
Offering one-on-one mentorship sessions for fellows struggling with specific procedural competencies.
Establish Timelines:
Set realistic timelines for the implementation of changes. For example:

Continuous Monitoring:
Regularly track the progress of the action plan through quarterly reviews.
Measure the effectiveness of interventions using follow-up surveys and performance metrics.
Adjustments Based on Feedback:
Adapt the action plan based on feedback from ongoing evaluations. For example, if faculty development initiatives do not result in improved mentorship, revisit and refine the training offered.

Recommendations for continued improvements.

The FMIGS program will adhere to a structured, data-driven process of continuous quality improvement. This includes a consistent evaluation of fellow performance, faculty mentorship, and training outcomes, ensuring that the program evolves to meet emerging challenges and remains aligned with the highest standards of minimally invasive gynecologic surgery.

22. Disciplinary Action
Types of Disciplinary Actions
Official disciplinary actions are probation, non-reappointment, or termination. In
general, disciplinary action should follow the due process identified by the primary
training site as is commonly distributed by the Department of Graduate Education.
If any type of disciplinary action is taken, the FMIGS Board must be notified.
The FMIGS Board requires the following sequence:
The fellow must be advised about deficiencies and the expectations for
improvement must be clearly delineated. This must occur every semi-annual
evaluation, but also may occur in an interval meeting if needed. The ability to
provide useful feedback is contingent upon regularly completed written
evaluations of the trainee. The fellowship director needs to provide clear guidance
to the training faculty as to the types and frequencies of evaluations expected
from them. Verbal feedback from a faculty member to the fellowship director
regarding a trainee, either positive or negative, must be followed up with a written
communication for the trainee’s file.
When a trainee has been advised about deficiencies but fails to make sufficient
improvement, he/she may be warned that continued lack of improvement may
result in probation. This information must be provided to the trainee in person
The objective of academic discipline is remediation. Thus, the terms of probation
should always be carefully devised to ensure that the trainee can attain the
desired improvement and that methods for evaluating that improvement are
robust and as objective as possible.
Clearly suboptimal academic and/or clinical performance may warrant probation.
The action must be explained to the fellow in person and in writing. Expectations
for improvement, the methods for evaluating improvement, the anticipated
duration of probation, and possible future actions must be delineated. The trainee
must be advised that their academic file is always available for review and that
he/she may appeal the decision. The trainee should be offered counseling. A
sample probationary letter is available from the FMIGS Board but is subject to local variation.
A trainee’s failure to remediate suboptimal academic and/or clinical performance
may warrant a decision not to reappoint the trainee at the end of the current
training year, or, in unusual circumstances, to terminate the contract immediately.
The action must be explained to the fellow member in person and in writing. As
with a probationary letter, the trainee must be advised that their academic file is
always available for review and that he/she may appeal the decision. The trainee
must be offered counseling. A sample non-reappointment or termination letter is
available from the FMIGS Board but is subject to local variation.
Termination without an intervening period of probation should be reserved for a
serious deviation from acceptable academic and clinical performance (e.g.,
dereliction of duty) that endangers patient care.
A probationary period must be long enough to permit a thorough evaluation of
progress. Except in unusual circumstances, a period of at least 3-4 months is
required. The date on which the trainee’s status will be reconsidered should be picked considering possible future actions, such as non-reappointment, so that
ideally the trainee will have ample opportunity to find a different training program
before the end of the training year. Alternatively, if a trainee’s lack of progress
requires a period of probation late in the training year, there should be
consideration of extending the current training year until a decision regarding
adequacy of remediation can be made.

match without prior approval from the FMIGS Board. If a fellowship program
intends to accept a specific candidate outside the match (e.g., graduating resident
from their program), they must contact the FMIGS NRMP representative, obtain
FMIGS Board approval for the match waiver and avoid subjecting other candidates
to the unnecessary burdens of interviewing.
The match provides a uniform time for both applicants and fellowship programs
to make selection decisions without coercion, undue or unwarranted pressure.
Both applicants and fellowship programs may express their interest in each other;
however, they shall not solicit verbal or written statements implying a
commitment. Applicants shall always be free to keep confidential the names or
identities of programs to which they have or may apply. Any violations will be
addressed by the FMIGS Board and will be subject to consequences as determined
by the FMIGS Board.

23. Line-by-Line Program Requirements and Curriculum Alignment

This section provides a detailed line-by-line alignment of each program requirement (educational, procedural, and competency-based) with specific aspects of the curriculum that directly address these requirements. Each requirement is listed verbatim, followed by the corresponding curriculum components that fulfill it.
1. Patient Care
Program Requirement:

Fellows must be able to provide patient care that is compassionate, appropriate, and effective for the treatment of health problems and the promotion of health. Fellows must demonstrate competence in:
A) Evaluating a patient's complaint, providing an accurate examination, employing appropriate diagnostic tests, arriving at a correct diagnosis, and recommending the appropriate treatment
Curriculum Components Addressing this Requirement:
1. Clinical Rotations (Sections 12 and 13):

Direct Patient Care: During rotations at SFH, SJH, SMH, and TMH, fellows evaluate patients' complaints, perform physical examinations, order and interpret diagnostic tests (e.g., ultrasonography, CT, MRI), arrive at diagnoses, and recommend treatments.
Supervised Practice: Fellows work under the guidance of experienced faculty to refine their clinical skills.
2. Didactic Learning (Section 14):
Lectures on Diagnostic Techniques: Monthly didactic sessions cover patient evaluation methods, diagnostic testing, and clinical reasoning.
Case Conferences: Regular presentations and discussions of patient cases to enhance diagnostic acumen.
3. Simulation Training (Section 11):
Clinical Scenarios: Simulation labs provide practice in patient examination and diagnostic procedures in a controlled environment.
4. Assessment and Evaluation (Section 16):
Direct Observation: Faculty assess fellows during patient encounters.
Objective Structured Clinical Examinations (OSCEs): Fellows' clinical skills are evaluated in simulated patient interactions.
Feedback Mechanisms: Regular feedback sessions to discuss performance and areas for improvement.
B) The essential areas of benign gynecology including:
Normal physiology of reproductive tract
Curriculum Components Addressing this Requirement:
1. Didactic Learning (Section 14):
Lectures on Reproductive Physiology: Detailed sessions on the normal functioning of the female reproductive system.
FMIGS Core Reading List (Appendix N): Assigned readings on reproductive physiology.
2. Clinical Rotations:
Application in Patient Care: Fellows apply knowledge of normal physiology during patient evaluations and treatment planning.
3. Assessment:
Written Exams: Testing understanding of reproductive physiology.
Case Discussions: Demonstrating application of physiological knowledge in clinical scenarios.
Gynecologic management during pregnancy
Curriculum Components Addressing this Requirement:
1. Clinical Rotations:
Rotation in Obstetrics (Elective): Opportunity to manage gynecologic issues in pregnant patients.
High-Risk Clinics: Exposure to gynecologic conditions complicating pregnancy.
2. Didactic Learning:
Lectures on Pregnancy-related Gynecologic Care: Covering topics like cervical incompetence, adnexal masses in pregnancy, and surgical interventions.
3. Assessment:
Case Presentations: Fellows present cases involving pregnant patients with gynecologic conditions.
Faculty Feedback: Evaluations on management plans and understanding of risks.
Gynecologic surgery and complications management
Curriculum Components Addressing this Requirement:
1. Surgical Training (Sections 12 and 13):
Operative Experience: Performing gynecologic surgeries (e.g., hysterectomy, myomectomy) under supervision.
Exposure to Complications: Managing intraoperative and postoperative complications during rotations
2. Simulation Training (Section 11):
Complications Drills: Simulated scenarios of surgical complications (e.g., hemorrhage, injury to adjacent organs).
3. Didactic Learning:
Lectures on Surgical Techniques: Emphasizing prevention and management of complications.
Morbidity and Mortality Conferences: Reviewing cases with complications to learn from experiences.
4. Assessment:
Surgical Skill Evaluations: Faculty assess technical proficiency and response to complications.
Operative Logs: Tracking surgical cases and any complications encountered
Management of critically ill patients
Curriculum Components Addressing this Requirement:
1. Clinical Rotations:
Intensive Care Unit (ICU) Exposure: Fellows rotate through ICU settings, managing critically ill gynecologic patients.
Emergency Gynecology: Handling acute cases requiring immediate intervention.
2. Didactic Learning:
Critical Care Lectures: Topics include hemodynamic monitoring, sepsis management, and advanced life support.
3. Simulation Training:
Critical Care Scenarios: Practicing management of critical situations like shock, respiratory failure.
4. Assessment:
Performance in Critical Situations: Faculty evaluate decision-making and intervention skills.
Case Reviews: Analyzing management of critically ill patients.
Gynecologic pathology
Curriculum Components Addressing this Requirement:
1. Didactic Learning:
Pathology Lectures: Comprehensive coverage of gynecologic diseases.
Pathology Workshops: Interactive sessions with actual specimens and slides.
2. Clinical Rotations:
Pathology Department Collaboration: Reviewing histopathological findings of surgical specimens.
3. Assessment:
Pathology Quizzes: Testing knowledge of gynecologic pathology.
Case Correlation: Demonstrating understanding of pathology in patient management.

Curriculum Components Addressing this Requirement:
1. EMR Training:
Documentation Workshops: Best practices for medical record-keeping.
2. Clinical Practice:
Record Maintenance: Ensuring accurate and timely documentation.
3. Assessment:
Chart Audits: Reviewing records for completeness and accuracy.
F) Have the fundamentals of good medical history taking and thoughtful, meticulous physical examination
Curriculum Components Addressing this Requirement:
1. Clinical Training:
Bedside Teaching: Faculty guide fellows in history-taking and examination.
2. Simulation Labs:
Practice Sessions: Refining examination techniques.
3. Assessment:
Direct Observation: Faculty assess skills during patient encounters.
OSCEs: Testing proficiency in simulated settings.
5. Professionalism
Program Requirement:
Fellows must demonstrate a commitment to carrying out professional responsibilities and an adherence to ethical principles. Fellows are expected to demonstrate:
A) Compassion, integrity, and respect for others
Curriculum Components Addressing this Requirement:
1. Professionalism Workshops:
Ethics Training: Understanding ethical obligations.
2. Role Modeling:
Faculty Exemplars: Demonstrating professional behavior.
3. Assessment:
Professionalism Evaluations: Faculty assess conduct during clinical duties.
B) Responsiveness to patient needs that supersedes self-interest
Curriculum Components Addressing this Requirement:
1. Patient-Centered Care Emphasis:
Curriculum Focus: Prioritizing patient well-being in all activities
2. Assessment:
Feedback from Patients and Families: Evaluating commitment to patient needs.
C) Respect for patient privacy and autonomy
Curriculum Components Addressing this Requirement:
1. HIPAA Training:
Privacy Regulations: Understanding legal requirements.
2. Clinical Practice:
Confidentiality Protocols: Implementing best practices.
3. Assessment:
Compliance Audits: Ensuring adherence to privacy standards.
D) Accountability to patients, society, and the profession
Curriculum Components Addressing this Requirement:
1. Professional Responsibility Discussions:
Seminars on Medical Professionalism: Exploring duties and obligations.
2. Assessment:
Peer and Faculty Evaluations: Assessing reliability and accountability.
E) Sensitivity and responsiveness to a diverse patient population, including but not limited to diversity in gender, age, culture, race, religion, disabilities, and sexual orientation
Curriculum Components Addressing this Requirement:
1. Diversity Training:
Workshops on Cultural Competence: Addressing biases and promoting inclusivity.
2. Clinical Exposure:
Serving Diverse Communities: Rotations in varied settings.
3. Assessment:
Cultural Competence Evaluations: Feedback on interactions with diverse patients.
F) Ethics and medical jurisprudence
Curriculum Components Addressing this Requirement:
1. Ethics Education:
Lectures on Medical Law: Understanding legal aspects of practice.
2. Case Studies:
Ethical Dilemmas: Analyzing and discussing real-world scenarios.
3. Assessment:
Ethics Exams: Testing knowledge of ethical principles and laws.
6. Systems-Based Practice
Program Requirement:

Fellows must demonstrate an awareness of and responsiveness to the larger context and system of health care, as well as the ability to call effectively on other resources in the system to provide optimal health care.
A) Work effectively in various health care delivery settings and systems relevant to their clinical specialty
Curriculum Components Addressing this Requirement:
1. Clinical Rotations in Multiple Settings:
Exposure to Different Systems: Rotations at SFH, SJH, SMH, and TMH offer experience in various healthcare environments.
2. Health Systems Education:
Lectures on Healthcare Delivery: Understanding different models and settings.
3. Assessment:
Faculty Evaluations: Assessing adaptability and effectiveness in different settings.
B) Coordinate patient care within the health care system relevant to their clinical specialty
Curriculum Components Addressing this Requirement:
1. Interdisciplinary Collaboration:
Team-Based Care: Working with various healthcare professionals to manage patient care.
2. Case Management:
Coordinating Services: Ensuring patients receive necessary resources and follow-up.
3. Assessment:
Case Reviews: Evaluating coordination efforts.
C) Incorporate considerations of cost awareness and risk-benefit analysis in patient and/or population-based care as appropriate
Curriculum Components Addressing this Requirement:
1. Health Economics Education:
Lectures on Cost-Effective Care: Understanding healthcare costs and resource allocation.
2. Clinical Decision-Making:
Risk-Benefit Analysis: Applying this in treatment planning.
3. Assessment:
Case Discussions: Evaluating consideration of costs and benefits.
D) Advocate for quality patient care and optimal patient care systems
Curriculum Components Addressing this Requirement:
1. Quality Improvement Projects:
Initiatives to Enhance Care: Fellows lead projects aiming to improve patient care systems.
2. Policy Education:
Understanding Healthcare Policies: Impact on patient care.
3. Assessment:
Project Outcomes: Evaluated for effectiveness
E) Work in inter-professional teams to enhance patient safety and improve patient care quality
Curriculum Components Addressing this Requirement:
1. Team Training:
Interprofessional Education Sessions: Collaborating with other healthcare disciplines.
2. Patient Safety Initiatives:
Participation in Safety Committees: Addressing systemic issues.
3. Assessment:
Team Performance Evaluations: Feedback on collaborative efforts.
F) Participate in identifying system errors and implementing potential systems solutions
Curriculum Components Addressing this Requirement:
1. Error Reporting Training:
Learning Systems for Reporting: Encouraging a culture of safety.
2. Quality Improvement Participation:
Analyzing Errors: Implementing solutions to prevent recurrence.
3. Assessment:
QI Project Evaluations: Measuring impact on system improvements.

FMIGS Fellowship Checklist: Yearly Timeline of Tasks
Select Fellows for the Program:
Use the NRMP Matching Process for fellowship selection (as required by FMIGS).
Notify fellows of start date (no later than August 1st).
Ensure candidates are aware of all program policies, benefits, and requirements, including travel to meetings (AAGL/ASRM), insurance, and the potential for non-compete agreements.
Review and Confirm Fellowship Director and Faculty:
Ensure the Fellowship Director and faculty meet FMIGS qualifications.
Identify at least one Associate Program Director.
Finalize Program Letter of Agreement (PLA) if more than one clinical site is used.
Prepare Didactic and Clinical Schedules:
Develop a detailed yearly schedule for clinical rotations, surgical training, didactic lectures, and simulation training for Year 1 and Year 2 fellows.
Ensure simulation and skills training are integrated into the schedule.
Onboarding and Orientation:
Introduce fellows to program policies, duty hours, and program structure.
Provide access to relevant facilities and resources (e.g., clinical information systems, libraries, simulation labs).
Assign Research Mentors:
Assign each fellow a research mentor who will guide them through their research project, starting in Year 1.
Ensure research mentors are meeting regularly with fellows.
Begin Surgical Competency Development:
Begin assessing fellows using the FMIGS Surgical Competency List (Appendix 4). Include mild/moderate cases of laparoscopic adhesiolysis, ovarian surgery, hysteroscopy, and diagnostic laparoscopy.
Establish Case Log Tracking:
Ensure fellows begin entering all surgical cases through the online data collection system.
Conduct a review to ensure fellows understand case logging requirements and deadlines.
Research Project Initiation:
Ensure each fellow has submitted a research project proposal.
Fellows should complete at least one course in research design, biostatistics, or epidemiology.
First Semi-Annual Evaluation (December – January):
Conduct semi-annual evaluations for each fellow, assessing:
Competence in patient care, medical knowledge, and surgical skills.
Professionalism and interpersonal communication.
Research progress (evaluation of research design and early data collection).
Use multiple evaluators (faculty, peers, and patients) and document evaluations in writing.
Program Evaluation:
Conduct an internal program evaluation with faculty and at least one fellow in attendance.
Discuss program strengths and weaknesses, review fellow performance, and faculty performance.
Use the findings to make improvements to the program.
Continue Surgical Training and Case Log Review:
Focus on progressing from simple laparoscopic procedures to advanced laparoscopic and robotic surgeries (e.g., laparoscopic myomectomy, endometriosis excision).
Monitor each fellow’s surgical case volume to ensure they are on track to meet FMIGS case requirements.
Mid-Year Case Log Review:
Conduct a mid-year review of fellows’ case logs and surgical competencies.
Identify any gaps in case volume or experience and adjust the clinical rotation schedule accordingly.
Research Project Progress:
Ensure each fellow has made significant progress in data collection for their research project.
Mentor feedback should be provided on research methodology, data analysis, and manuscript preparation.
Prepare for Annual Report Submission (Due July 1st):
Ensure the following are ready for the Annual Report:
Fellow’s case logs are up to date.
Research project updates are included (progress on original data-driven research).
A summary of faculty periodic evaluations of the program.
Submit annual report to the FMIGS Board, including evaluations, fellow progress, and clinical experience.
Second Semi-Annual Evaluation (June – July):
Conduct the second semi-annual evaluation of fellows, focusing on:
Surgical competency, including robotic surgeries and advanced laparoscopic techniques.
Progress in research project (manuscript or conference submission).
Completion of clinical and didactic requirements.
Documentation of progressive improvement in patient care and medical knowledge.
Duty Hours Monitoring:
Monitor duty hours according to program policy and ensure compliance with ACGME guidelines.
Provide back-up systems if fellows experience fatigue or excessive service demands.
Faculty Evaluations:
Conduct annual evaluations of all faculty members, assessing:
Clinical teaching ability.
Commitment to the educational program.
Scholarly activities and professionalism.
Program Evaluation by Fellows:
Gather anonymous feedback from fellows regarding the program structure, clinical experiences, and teaching quality.
Monthly Didactic Sessions:
Schedule structured teaching conferences and seminars, focusing on core topics such as pelvic anatomy, endometriosis management, and advanced surgical techniques.
Ensure fellows have time for self-directed learning and can attend national conferences.
Simulation Training:
Regularly schedule skills labs for laparoscopic and robotic surgery simulation, ensuring fellows gain hands-on experience before performing on real patients.
Case Conferences:
Hold weekly case conferences where fellows present complex cases and receive feedback on their decision-making and surgical planning.
Completion of Surgical Competency Requirements:
Verify that fellows have completed the minimum number of surgical cases across core areas (e.g., laparoscopy, robotic surgery, hysteroscopy).
Ensure that the FMIGS Surgical Competency List has been completed and signed off for each fellow.
Research Completion:
Ensure that each fellow has completed an original research project and submitted a manuscript for publication or presented at a national conference.
Final Summative Evaluation:
Conduct a final summative evaluation for each fellow, documenting their overall performance, competency, and readiness for independent practice.
Submit Final Certification Request:
Once all requirements are met, submit a request for the fellow’s certification to the FMIGS Board.
This checklist ensures that the FMIGS fellowship program adheres to all program requirements, including timely evaluations, research progress, case volume tracking, and competency assessments.
